signals: has no tool that grants one
stem: Skarsby Air's support agent resolves 62% of contacts on first touch against an 85% target. Transcript review shows two opposite errors: it hands routine rebooking questions to human staff, yet keeps working fare-rule exceptions itself, cycling through standard options until the customer gives up. Only supervisors can approve an exception, and the agent has no tool that grants one, so a late handoff costs goodwill but moves no money. The system prompt currently says only 'escalate when appropriate'.
ask: Which change BEST calibrates when the agent escalates?

options.text: Ask the agent to score its own certainty as a percentage on each turn and hand off whenever it falls below 60%
options.why: Self-rated certainty is poorly calibrated, and this agent errs in both directions: sure of itself on exceptions, hesitant on routine rebookings. A cutoff on that number would reproduce the same misroutes with extra ceremony.

options.text: Write explicit escalation criteria by case type into the system prompt, with examples to hand off and resolve
options.why: Both failures trace to an undefined boundary, since 'when appropriate' gives the agent nothing to apply. Naming the case types that belong to supervisors, with contrasting examples on each side, fixes the decision at its source, and a miss here stays recoverable.

options.text: Escalate automatically whenever the customer repeats the same request twice within a single conversation
options.why: This treats repetition as a stand-in for case type. It fires only after the customer has been cycled through options, so the goodwill is already spent; it can add handoffs but never remove the needless rebooking ones; and a customer repeating a simple question would be escalated too.

options.text: Move the agent to a more capable model tier so it can recognise complex cases without any further instructions
options.why: The defect is a missing specification, not missing capability. Any tier told to 'escalate when appropriate' still has to guess where a supervisor's authority starts, so the upgrade adds cost without defining the boundary.

explain: Binding constraint: fare exceptions are a supervisor's decision, and the agent has never been told where that boundary sits. Route escalation by case type and consequence, written as explicit criteria with examples, never by the model's self-rated certainty or a behavioural proxy such as repetition; no hard gate is needed because the agent cannot grant an exception anyway.

stem: Inchbrook Press runs a research system in which a coordinator sends questions to a web-search subagent and passes its findings to a synthesis subagent that drafts the briefing. While drafting, the synthesis agent often needs a claim checked, and each check goes back through the coordinator to the search agent, adding several round trips and roughly a third to end-to-end latency. Logs show 70% of checks are single-figure lookups, such as a date or a statistic; 30% need a genuine new investigation. The editors want the synthesis agent to stay a drafting role, not a second researcher.
ask: Which configuration change BEST reduces the overhead while keeping verification reliable?

options.text: Queue every verification need and send the whole list to the coordinator once the synthesis pass is finished
options.why: Queuing assumes the draft does not depend on the checks. In practice the briefing is written on unverified claims, any failed check forces a rewrite, and verification becomes a blocking step at the end, so latency moves rather than falls.

options.text: Give the synthesis agent the full set of web-search tools so it can run any check itself with no round trips
options.why: This removes the round trips by handing a drafting role the open-ended search the editors want kept out of it. Tool choice gets harder, the agent can drift into new research instead of synthesising, and the common case needed only a single lookup.

options.text: Give the synthesis agent a narrow lookup_figure tool and keep deeper checks routed through the coordinator
options.why: A scoped lookup covers the 70% case inside the agent and removes most of the round trips, while real investigations keep their existing path. The agent gains one narrow capability rather than open-ended search, so it stays a drafting role.

options.text: Let the synthesis agent message the search agent directly for each check, bypassing the coordinator
options.why: Direct messaging trims one hop, but every one-figure lookup still costs a full search-agent turn, so most of the latency stays. It also takes checks out of the coordinator's view, so no single component tracks, retries or logs verification.

explain: Binding constraint: least privilege under a latency target. Give a role the narrowest capability that covers its common case and leave the rare, heavier path where it already lives; that removes most of the round trips without widening what the synthesis agent can do or taking checks out of the coordinator's view.

signals: about a third are simple lookups
stem: Fennimore University's library runs a research assistant in which a coordinator sends every question through four subagents in turn: web search, document analysis, synthesis and report writing. Most traffic is complex literature questions, but about a third are simple lookups such as 'What is the loan period for a reserve-collection book?'. Those take around 45 seconds and cost as much as a full literature review. Several of the hardest questions last term were under ten words, such as 'Is sleep linked to GPA?'. The service owner wants simple questions answered quickly without weakening the complex ones.
ask: Which design change BEST meets the service owner's goal?

options.text: Add a keyword table ahead of the coordinator that sends short, lookup-style queries straight to a single call
options.why: Routing by complexity is sound, but a keyword table judges difficulty by surface wording. Last term's hardest questions included one-line queries such as the sleep and GPA question, which a table would send down the simple path, weakening exactly the complex answers the owner wants protected.

options.text: Let each subagent judge its own relevance to the question and opt in or out of the pipeline as the query runs
options.why: Adding autonomy to every subagent means each one must still read the query to decide, so cost stays high, and no single component owns the routing decision or can explain why a path was taken.

options.text: Merge web search and document analysis into one retrieval subagent so every question passes through three stages
options.why: Merging two stages trims some latency but still sends a one-line lookup through a multi-stage pipeline, and it weakens the complex path by blending two distinct retrieval jobs into one agent.

options.text: Have the coordinator triage questions: one model call with retrieval for simple ones, subagents for the rest
options.why: Triage matches the pattern to the request: a simple lookup needs one augmented call with retrieval and no agents, while a model reading the question's meaning can still send a short but hard research question to the subagents. Both of the service owner's goals are met.

explain: Binding constraint: latency and cost on simple requests without weakening complex ones. Choose the simplest pattern that works for each request; a one-step lookup gets a single augmented LLM call, and agents are kept for questions whose path cannot be listed in advance.

signals: close_account ran before identity was confirmed
stem: Dunmere Savings runs a support agent that closes accounts on request. The procedure is: confirm identity with get_customer, check linked products with check_linked_products, then call close_account. Last quarter's logs show a handful of cases where close_account ran before identity was confirmed, including two accounts the caller did not own. A closed account cannot be reopened online. A colleague proposes adding 'Always verify identity before closing an account' to the system prompt.
ask: Which approach BEST ensures an account is closed only after its owner has been verified?

options.text: Make close_account refuse to run unless get_customer has verified the caller as this account's owner in the session
options.why: The check lives in the tool, outside the model, and binds the closure to the verified caller's own account, so neither an unverified closure nor a closure of someone else's account can run whatever the agent decides. It still holds if the model ignores its instructions completely.

options.text: Adopt the prompt rule and add few-shot examples that walk through all three steps in the correct order each time
options.why: Examples raise the odds of the right order, but the logs already show the agent skipping a step it was expected to follow. For an irreversible closure, a better success rate is still a failure rate.

options.text: Log each close_account call and alert the fraud team whenever no identity check was recorded beforehand
options.why: The alert reaches the fraud team after the account is already closed, and it cannot be reopened online. Detection is a useful second layer, but the ask is to stop the closure, not to find out about it.

options.text: Move the agent to a stronger reasoning model that follows multi-step procedures more reliably in production
options.why: Out-of-order calls are a control defect, not a capability gap. A stronger model still follows instructions probabilistically, so wrongful closures become rarer at higher cost but remain possible.

explain: Binding constraint: the order must hold every time because a wrongful closure is irreversible. Enforce it with a prerequisite check outside the model that refuses close_account until get_customer has verified the caller as the owner of that account; prompts and examples only raise the odds, and alerts arrive after the damage.

signals: refunds above $500 need a manager's approval
stem: Ormsby Trail Supply's support agent issues refunds through a process_refund tool. Policy says refunds above $500 need a manager's approval, and the system prompt states this rule plainly. Audit sampling finds the agent paid about 3% of over-limit refunds on its own. Refunds reach the customer's card within minutes and are rarely recovered once paid. Managers are happy to review high-value cases but refuse to approve every refund, which would bury them in routine $20 returns.
ask: Which design BEST places the human approval where the policy needs it?

options.text: Rewrite the prompt rule in stronger terms, stating that over-limit refunds are forbidden without explicit approval
options.why: Stronger wording nudges the odds, but the rule is already stated plainly and still fails about 3% of the time. Money leaves within minutes, so a control that depends on the model choosing to comply is not enough.

options.text: Intercept process_refund before it runs and hold every refund, whatever its amount, for a manager to approve
options.why: This places the gate correctly but ignores the threshold. Managers have said they will not approve every refund, and sending each $20 return to them buries the high-value cases in routine volume and invites click-through approvals, a paper gate.

options.text: Intercept process_refund before it runs and hold any amount over $500 in a manager approval queue
options.why: The interception sits outside the model and acts before money moves, so no over-limit refund can skip the manager, while routine returns below the threshold flow without review. In an agent framework this is typically a pre-tool-use hook.

options.text: Run a check after each process_refund call that reverses any refund above $500 lacking a recorded approval
options.why: Reversal acts after the payout, and paid refunds are rarely recovered. An after-the-fact check is useful for audit, but the policy calls for approval before the action, not cleanup once the money has gone.

explain: Binding constraint: a paid refund is effectively irreversible, so the human gate must sit before the action and apply every time, but only above the policy threshold. Put a control point outside the model that intercepts process_refund and routes over-limit amounts to a manager, gating by amount rather than reviewing everything or relying on prompt wording.

signals: no one can say in advance which logs, configs or commits will matter
stem: Lumen Ledger, a payments software provider, has a production defect that began sometime in the last two weeks. Symptoms appear in three services, but the change behind it could sit in any of a dozen repositories owned by five teams, and no one can say in advance which logs, configs or commits will matter. The investigation is read-only: Claude can read code, logs and deploy history, and an engineer reviews and approves any fix before it ships.
ask: Which architecture pattern BEST fits this investigation?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain that checks logs, then configs, then service traces in the same order on every incident
options.why: A fixed chain assumes the path is known in advance. Here nobody can list which logs, configs or commits matter, so the chain runs the same checks every time and cannot follow a lead into an unexpected service.

options.text: An agentic loop that maps symptoms and deploy history, then plans each next check from what it has found
options.why: Both conditions for an agent hold: the path emerges only as evidence arrives, and a wrong intermediate step is cheap because the work is read-only and an engineer approves any fix before it ships.

options.text: One agent per service-owning team, each examining its own repositories and reporting to the on-call lead
options.why: Each agent searches only its own team's repositories, so a symptom in one service cannot lead it to a commit in another team's code. Linking is left to a person reading separate reports after the fact, and nobody follows the lead across the seam.

options.text: A single pass that searches every commit from the two weeks and returns a ranked list of suspects for review
options.why: Ranking commits in one pass judges each change on its own text. It cannot follow evidence from a symptom in one service to a config change in another, which is the reasoning this defect demands.

explain: Binding constraint: the investigation path cannot be listed in advance, because it emerges from each finding. Mistakes along the way are recoverable, since the work is read-only and fixes need an engineer's approval, which makes an agent acceptable. That combination justifies an agentic loop, or orchestrator-workers, over a fixed workflow; a fixed chain, a team split or a one-shot search is under-built here.

signals: launching fresh searches instead of synthesising
text copied from external web pages
stem: Tallis Therapeutics built a literature-review system in which search subagents gather papers, check each claim, and hand verified findings to a synthesis agent that turns them into a structured evidence report. To keep it flexible, the synthesis agent was given all 18 tools in the system, including web search, database queries, email sending and calendar access. Reviewers now see it launching fresh searches instead of synthesising what it was handed, and the findings it reads include text copied from external web pages.
ask: Which change BEST addresses the risks in this configuration?

options.text: Add a paragraph to the system prompt telling the synthesis agent which tools to use for each part of its job
options.why: A routing paragraph asks the model to ignore capabilities it still holds, and choosing among 18 tools stays hard. Email also remains within reach of any instruction injected through the copied web text.

options.text: Keep all 18 tools but require a human confirmation before the synthesis agent sends email or books a meeting
options.why: Confirmation guards a capability the role never needs. Synthesis has no reason to send email or book meetings, so removal is the right move, and the confirmation does nothing about the off-role searches.

options.text: Shorten every tool description to cut the input tokens that 18 schemas add to each synthesis request
options.why: Eighteen schemas do add input tokens, cost and a little time to first token, but that is secondary. Terser descriptions make tool choice harder, and neither the off-role searches nor the email exposure changes.

options.text: Limit the synthesis agent to its role's tools, removing open-ended search, the database, email and calendar
options.why: Scoping the toolset to the role fixes both findings: without open-ended search the agent works from the verified findings it was handed, and without email, injected text in those findings has no path to send data out.

explain: Binding constraint: least privilege for a role that only combines findings it is given. Tools outside a role's job degrade tool selection and widen the blast radius when untrusted text reaches the agent, so remove those capabilities rather than guarding or re-describing them; the token overhead is real but secondary.

signals: sampled at random from last quarter's intake
stem: Norrow Insurance extracts 22 fields from claim documents with Claude. Intake spans six claim types, from auto glass to commercial property, and some fields, such as claim_amount and policy_number, drive payments directly. On a validation set of 4,000 claims sampled at random from last quarter's intake, with at least 300 claims of each type, 97% of extracted fields are correct. The company handles about 60,000 claims a month, and the team proposes removing human review.
ask: What should the team establish FIRST before removing review?

options.text: Accuracy by claim type and by field, including payment fields such as claim_amount and policy_number
options.why: Per-slice scores show whether a rare claim type or a payment field such as claim_amount sits far below the headline. A slice at 85% can sit inside 97% overall, and that slice decides whether review can go.

options.text: The monthly error count implied by 97%, about 40,000 wrong fields a month, to size the legal exposure
options.why: Converting a rate to a count is a good habit, but it still treats errors as spread evenly. It says nothing about which claim types or fields fail, so it cannot show where review is still needed.

options.text: Whether the validation set reflects the production mix of claim types, since a skewed set would inflate 97%
options.why: Representativeness matters, but the set was sampled at random from last quarter's intake, so its mix already tracks production, and every type has enough claims to score. The open question is how accuracy varies inside that mix, not whether the mix is right.

options.text: A standing rule that insurance claims keep full human review whatever the measured accuracy turns out to be
options.why: A blanket rule ignores the evidence the team is about to gather. Full review of routine, accurate slices wastes reviewer attention and drifts into rubber-stamping; review belongs where errors concentrate.

explain: Binding constraint: payment-driving fields need an accuracy floor on every slice, not on the average. Score the evaluation set per claim type and per field before removing review, because a strong aggregate can hide the failing slice the decision depends on.

signals: even if injected text in a ticket persuades it to try
Its only file-modifying tool is write_file
stem: Quarrystone Energy runs a maintenance agent, built with an agent SDK, that edits files in a grid-operations repository. Its only file-modifying tool is write_file, and it has no shell. Security requires that nothing under config/production/ is ever changed by the agent, even if injected text in a ticket persuades it to try. A developer proposes a hook that runs after each tool call, logs every write and pages the on-call engineer when a protected path appears. The agent legitimately edits files elsewhere in the repository.
ask: Which control BEST meets the security requirement?

options.text: A post-execution hook that restores any protected file from version control as soon as a write to it lands
options.why: The file has already changed when the hook runs, and services may load the bad config before the restore. Reverting after the write crosses the boundary is cleanup, not the guarantee the requirement asks for.

options.text: A pre-execution check on write_file that resolves the canonical path and refuses targets in config/production/
options.why: Because write_file is the agent's only way to change files, a check before execution, such as a pre-tool-use hook, holds even when injected text convinces the model to try. Resolving the canonical path first means traversal or symlinks cannot disguise a protected target.

options.text: A firm system prompt prohibition on protected paths, with the proposed post-execution hook kept for auditing
options.why: A system prompt is not a security boundary, and the threat here is precisely injected text overriding instructions. The audit hook would record the breach after it happened but could not stop it.

options.text: Removal of write_file from the agent, with engineers applying each change it drafts by hand in the repository
options.why: The agent legitimately edits files outside the protected directory, so removal breaks the role to fix a narrow risk. Removal suits capabilities a role never needs; a scoped pre-execution deny covers this one.

explain: Binding constraint: a protected path must stay unchanged even under prompt injection, so the control must prevent rather than detect and must sit outside the model. A pre-execution check on the agent's only write path, matching the resolved canonical path, meets that; logging, reverting and prompt wording do not, and if the agent also had a shell the check would have to cover that path too.

signals: draft the notes from the classified list
running the three steps as parallel subagents
stem: The digital service team at Ellisford City Council publishes release notes for its permits portal every fortnight. The workflow has three steps: gather the pull requests merged since the last release tag, classify each one as a feature, fix or security change, and draft the notes from the classified list. A typical release has 60 to 90 pull requests. A developer proposes running the three steps as parallel subagents to cut the time the notes take.
ask: Which decomposition BEST fits this workflow?

options.text: Run all three steps as parallel subagents, since each is a distinct specialism the coordinator can merge
options.why: This assumes the steps are independent, but classification needs the gathered list and drafting needs the classifications. Parallel subagents would start later stages before their inputs exist and then have to wait or guess.

options.text: Run collection as an LLM subagent so it can judge which pull requests matter, then classify and draft in turn
options.why: Which pull requests merged since a tag is a fact the repository already holds. A model doing that lookup adds cost and a chance of silently dropping items, and nothing at that stage needs judgement.

options.text: Give one prompt the full diff of every merged pull request and ask it to classify and draft in a single pass
options.why: Ninety full diffs can run to hundreds of thousands of tokens per release, which invites skipped or shallow classifications in the middle of the list, and it discards the per-item independence that makes classification easy to parallelise and check.

options.text: Gather the pull requests with a plain git query, classify them in parallel, then draft the notes in one call
options.why: This follows the dependency graph: a deterministic query gathers the facts, the independent per-PR classifications run concurrently where parallelism is real, and one drafting call works from the complete classified list.

explain: Binding constraint: each stage consumes the previous stage's output, so the stages run in sequence and parallelism belongs inside a stage. Decompose by dependency and independence: facts come from code, independent items fan out, and dependent steps chain.

signals: error rate on the same form types is unchanged
the fixed record is written to the claims database
stem: Corvane Mutual uses Claude to extract fields from scanned claim forms. Extractions below a confidence threshold go to a review queue, where adjusters correct them and the fixed record is written to the claims database. Six months later the error rate on the same form types is unchanged. A weekly chart of queue volume is emailed to an operations distribution list. The claims operations lead wants to know why so much review effort has not made the system any better.
ask: Which change BEST turns the review effort into improvement?

options.text: Also send a sample of high-confidence extractions to adjusters so the queue catches confident errors too
options.why: Sampling confident outputs is worthwhile because it exposes confident errors the threshold never routes. On its own, though, it only sharpens the error estimate. Without corrections flowing into measurement and prompt changes, the model behaves exactly as before.

options.text: Score corrections as labelled data per field and form type, with a named owner who revises prompts and examples
options.why: Corrections are ground-truth labels on the cases the model finds hardest. Scoring them per field and form type shows where it fails, and a named owner turning those results into prompt and few-shot example changes is what closes the loop.

options.text: Raise the confidence threshold each quarter so a growing share of extractions is corrected before it is stored
options.why: A higher threshold sends more work to adjusters and raises cost, yet each correction is still only written to the database. The review grows without ever changing what the model does on the next form.

options.text: Chart per-field correction rates on a live dashboard and post an alert to the team channel whenever a rate rises
options.why: Per-field rates and alerts make the problem visible sooner, but visibility is not a loop. An alert to a shared channel names no owner and gives corrections no path into evals, prompts or examples, so the model keeps making the same errors.

explain: Binding constraint: the error rate has to fall, yet every correction ends in the claims database. A design is end-to-end only when outcomes flow back as labelled data to a named owner who changes prompts and examples; a dashboard, an alert or a larger queue leaves the loop open.

signals: a single sentence written during prototyping
stem: Tallowbrook Outfitters runs a customer support agent with exactly two tools, `get_customer` and `lookup_order`, and has no plans to add more. Production traces show the agent calling `get_customer` when shoppers ask where their order is. Each tool description is a single sentence written during prototyping, and both tools accept either an email address or an account number as the identifier. The team lead wants the most proportionate step before anyone proposes a larger redesign of the agent.
ask: What should the team do FIRST to improve tool selection?

options.text: Merge both tools into one `lookup_entity` tool that accepts any identifier and chooses the right backend itself
options.why: Merging hides the ambiguity inside one broader tool instead of resolving it, and the model still has to express intent through a vaguer interface. With only two tools the catalogue is not the problem; their unclear boundary is.

options.text: Put a keyword router in front of each turn that reads the message and pre-selects the tool the agent may call
options.why: A router is a new component to build and maintain, and keyword rules misfire on phrasings such as 'my account shows no delivery'. It might earn a place later, but it is not the proportionate first step for two tools.

options.text: Rewrite both descriptions to state accepted inputs, example queries and when to prefer each over the other
options.why: Descriptions are what the model reads when it chooses a tool. Stating inputs, example queries and the boundary against the sibling tool fixes the real ambiguity at almost no cost, which suits a small, stable set.

options.text: Add six to eight worked examples of correct tool selection to the system prompt, leaving both definitions as they are
options.why: Examples cover only the phrasings they show. The definitions the model reads when it picks a tool still leave unclear which one owns 'where is my order', so new phrasings keep misrouting. Fix the descriptions first; examples can supplement them later.

explain: Binding constraint: the catalogue is small and stable, so the defect is an unclear boundary between two tools, and sharpening the descriptions the model reads at selection time comes first. For large catalogues of dozens of tools the fix shifts to per-role scoping or deferred tool loading, because longer descriptions alone do not scale.

signals: fully covered by the sources returned for it
stem: Pellham Strategy Group runs a research system in which a coordinator breaks a brief into subtasks and delegates them to web-search, document-analysis and synthesis subagents. For a manufacturers' association brief on how higher energy prices are affecting European factories, every subagent reported success. Traces show that every subtask the coordinator created was fully covered by the sources returned for it, and the synthesis draft used everything it received. The client still complains that the report covers steel and chemicals in depth but says nothing about food processing, paper or ceramics.
ask: What is the MOST likely root cause?

options.text: The synthesis subagent has no instruction to detect coverage gaps across the findings it is handed
options.why: Synthesis used everything it received, so it did its job. A gap check there might flag the hole after the fact, but detecting the missing sectors downstream does not explain why they were never researched in the first place.

options.text: The web-search subagent writes queries that are too narrow and needs broader terms for the other sectors
options.why: This assumes search was asked to cover food processing, paper and ceramics. Every subtask it received was fully covered by its sources, so nothing in the traces shows those sectors were ever requested.

options.text: The coordinator split the brief too narrowly, so no subagent was ever assigned the missing sectors
options.why: Every downstream step fully covered what it was given, which rules those layers out. Missing coverage with successful subagents points to the plan itself: the decomposition never included the other sectors.

options.text: The document-analysis subagent applies a relevance filter strict enough to discard other-sector sources
options.why: Every subtask was fully covered by the sources returned for it, so no filter removed material a subtask needed. It cannot have discarded evidence on sectors that no subtask ever asked the system to find.

explain: Binding constraint: every subtask was fully covered and synthesis used everything, which eliminates the execution layers. Missed coverage is a decomposition defect, so the fix is in how the coordinator splits the brief, for example checking the plan against the brief's full scope before delegating.

signals: retry, rephrase, try another source or proceed with a noted gap
stem: Quillon Therapeutics prepares literature reviews with a coordinator-subagent research system: the coordinator delegates searching, document analysis and synthesis to separate subagents. During a review of a rare-disease pathway, the web-search subagent times out partway through a complex query. You are designing how failures like this are reported back, so that the coordinator can decide whether to retry, rephrase, try another source or proceed with a noted gap.
ask: Which failure-reporting design BEST supports recovery by the coordinator?

options.text: Return a structured error with the failure type, the query, any partial results and suggested alternative sources
options.why: Structured failure context lets the coordinator pick among the recovery paths it owns: retry, rephrase, switch to a suggested source or accept a documented gap. Partial results are kept rather than wasted, and the failure stays visible in the final review.

options.text: Retry with backoff inside the subagent, then report a generic 'search unavailable' status once retries run out
options.why: Bounded retries with backoff are reasonable inside the subagent. The flaw is collapsing the outcome into an opaque status, which hides the failure type and partial results the coordinator needs to rephrase, switch source or accept a noted gap.

options.text: Catch the timeout in the subagent and return an empty result marked as success so the review keeps moving
options.why: Marking an empty result as success is a reassuring claim the system cannot back. The coordinator believes the search simply found nothing, so the review can ship with a silent gap that nobody knows to disclose or fix.

options.text: Pass the timeout up to a top-level handler that stops the whole review and pages the on-call engineer
options.why: Stopping everything assumes one timeout invalidates the whole review, which the stem does not grant. It throws away whatever the search had gathered and the other subagents' work when a local recovery was available.

explain: Binding constraint: the coordinator owns recovery, so it needs the failure type, the query and any partial results. Bounded retries inside the subagent are fine, but the outcome must return as structured context rather than an opaque status, a false success or a workflow-wide stop.

signals: blocking pre-merge review that developers wait on
compiled on Friday evening for Monday's planning meeting
the only commitment is a 24-hour window
stem: Fernhill Software's platform team runs two Claude workflows: a blocking pre-merge review that developers wait on before they can merge, and a technical-debt digest compiled on Friday evening for Monday's planning meeting. The review's current catch rate is the agreed quality bar. Their engineering manager, who owns the budget, proposes moving both to the Message Batches API to halve the per-token cost. Most batches finish within an hour, but the only commitment is a 24-hour window, after which unfinished requests expire. The manager has asked you for a recommendation she can approve this week.
ask: Which recommendation BEST fits both workflows?

options.text: Move both workflows to batches and poll for completion, since most batches come back well within an hour
options.why: Typical completion time is not a commitment. A blocking gate needs a latency guarantee, and the batch window only promises up to 24 hours, so any slow batch leaves developers unable to merge for hours.

options.text: Batch the weekly digest and move the pre-merge review to a smaller, cheaper model tier to save on it as well
options.why: Splitting the workflows is right, but nothing shows a smaller tier holds the agreed catch rate. This trades review quality for savings without evidence, and the manager would be approving a quality drop she never saw measured.

options.text: Move both workflows to batches with a timeout that falls back to a real-time call when a batch runs long
options.why: Developers still wait out the timeout before the fallback fires, and every fallback pays the full real-time price. The blocking path gets slower and more complex for a saving that shrinks exactly when batches run long.

options.text: Batch the weekly digest, keep the pre-merge review on real-time calls, and show the manager the trade-off
options.why: The digest is non-interactive and has a whole weekend of slack, well beyond the 24-hour window, so it takes the discount safely. The blocking review keeps real-time latency and its current model, and framing the split as money saved against developer time protected gives the manager a clear decision.

explain: Binding constraint: the pre-merge check blocks developers, so it needs guaranteed latency that a 24-hour batch window cannot give, and its catch rate must hold. Batch only non-interactive work with slack beyond 24 hours, such as the weekly digest, match results by custom_id, and present the split to the budget owner as cost saved against developer time protected.

signals: without asking developers to change how they work
stem: Harrowgate Retail's automated code review runs Claude once over each pull request. A recent change touched 22 files across the checkout and payments services, and the single-pass review was uneven: careful comments on the files near the top of the diff, little more than style notes on the rest, a missing input-validation check on a payment form overlooked, and conflicting naming advice for the same shared type in two files. The engineering lead wants consistent depth on every file without asking developers to change how they work.
ask: How should the review be restructured?

options.text: Require developers to split large pull requests into groups of three or four files before review runs
options.why: Smaller pull requests would help, but the stem rules out changing how developers work, and the review would still degrade whenever a large change lands. The fix belongs in how the review itself is structured.

options.text: Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window so a single pass covers all 22 files properly
options.why: Uneven depth across many files is a structural defect, not a capacity one. A bigger window still asks one pass to cover 22 files at once, so attention stays diluted on any tier.

options.text: Review each file in its own focused pass, then run a separate integration pass for cross-file consistency
options.why: Per-file passes give every file the same focused attention, and a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues such as the conflicting naming advice for the shared type. This is sectioning, then a chained integration step.

options.text: Run three independent passes over the whole pull request and report only issues that at least two runs flag
options.why: Majority voting filters out real bugs that only some runs catch, which is how a single missed validation check slips through. It also triples cost while each run still suffers the same shallow coverage.

explain: Binding constraint: every file needs consistent depth without changing developer behaviour, which is a structural problem. Decompose the review by sectioning it into independent per-file passes (a parallelisation pattern), then chain a cross-file integration pass, rather than enlarging the model or voting on shallow runs.

stem: Northwold Energy's market-research agent appends every tool result to its conversation history before the next request. A teammate proposes storing each full result in a database keyed by ID and giving the model only a short summary at each iteration, to cut tokens and keep the window focused. A typical job gathers tariff tables from several regulators and recommends which region to prioritise.
ask: Under which condition would this change MOST likely degrade the agent's decisions?

options.text: When long error traces from calls the agent has already retried are each reduced to a single summary line
options.why: Losing detail sounds risky, but traces from calls that were already retried have done their job. Keeping them verbatim only adds tokens and noise, and a one-line note costs nothing because no later step depends on the trace.

options.text: When the recommendation rests on exact figures from several results that the summaries paraphrase
options.why: Summaries keep the gist and drop exact values. When the recommendation depends on weighing specific tariff figures across results, those dropped values are exactly what the reasoning needs, so decisions degrade unless raw results can be re-fetched.

options.text: When the raw results reach the model only through an extra tool call that fetches them by ID
options.why: The extra call sounds like a hurdle, but it assumes summarised means lost. With raw results retrievable by ID, the agent keeps a lean context and pulls exact detail just in time, which is the mitigation that makes external storage safe.

options.text: When each request drops from tens of thousands of tokens of history to just a few thousand tokens
options.why: A large cut sounds dangerous, but shrinking the window is the purpose of the change and usually sharpens recall. A structured summary is not blind truncation; the risk lies in which details a later step needs, not in the token count.

explain: Binding constraint: the recommendation depends on exact values spread across several tariff tables. Storing results externally and passing summaries is a sanctioned context-engineering pattern that degrades decisions only when needed detail is paraphrased away, so keep raw results retrievable by ID for just-in-time re-fetch.

signals: cannot be traced to a source
stem: A policy unit at Ostvale Regional Council runs a research system in which a web-search subagent gathers findings and a synthesis subagent writes cited briefing papers for councillors. Reviewers keep finding briefings whose claims cannot be traced to a source, or cite a page that says something else. Traces show the search subagent returns a prose paragraph of findings followed by an unordered list of URLs, and the synthesis subagent then guesses which URL supports which claim.
ask: Which change BEST fixes the problem where it starts?

options.text: Have the search subagent return claim records, each with its URL, date and passage, passed on intact
options.why: Structured claim records keep each claim bound to its evidence across the handoff, so synthesis cites what it received instead of guessing. Citations then make every claim checkable, though reviewers still verify that each source supports it.

options.text: Add a line to the synthesis prompt requiring a specific source to be cited for every claim it writes
options.why: A prompt cannot restore a claim-to-source link that the handoff already destroyed. Told to cite every claim, the synthesis subagent will still guess from the URL list and produce confident but mismatched citations.

options.text: Let the synthesis subagent rerun the searches itself so it can find a source for each claim before writing
options.why: Searching again duplicates work, costs more, and can surface different sources from the ones behind the original findings. The defect sits in the handoff format, not in whether synthesis is able to search.

options.text: Have the search subagent return the full page text for every URL so synthesis can match claims to sources
options.why: More evidence arrives, but claims and sources are still unlinked. Synthesis now has to search whole pages to guess which one backs each finding, so mismatched citations remain and the context fills with text it mostly does not need.

explain: Binding constraint: every claim in a briefing must trace to a source, so provenance has to survive the handoff between subagents. Define a structured handoff contract of claim, source, date and passage, and remember that citations make claims checkable, not correct.

signals: do not depend on each other
has to complete before any confirmation is sent
stem: Kestrel Mobile's support agent receives one message with three requests: dispute a roaming charge, trace a handset order that never arrived, and change the account's email address. Each takes a few minutes, so handled one after another the reply takes about ten minutes. The billing check, the order trace and the email change use different systems and do not depend on each other. Company policy, however, says every resolution notice must go to the account's current email, so the address change has to complete before any confirmation is sent.
ask: Which design cuts response time MOST without breaking the policy?

options.text: Run all three requests in parallel from the shared account context and confirm each one as soon as it finishes
options.why: This treats the confirmations as independent of the email change, which the policy rules out. A billing or order confirmation could reach the old address before the change lands, breaking the resolution-notice policy.

options.text: Run the charge check, order trace and email change in parallel, holding all confirmations until the email updates
options.why: All three steps are independent, so they run as parallel sections, while the one real dependency is respected by gating confirmations on the email change. The reply takes about as long as the slowest step and every notice reaches the current address.

options.text: Run the charge check and order trace in parallel, then make the email change and send every confirmation once it is done
options.why: This keeps the policy but assumes the email change must wait for the investigations, which the stem says it does not. Leaving it until afterwards adds a serial step of a few minutes, so the reply is slower than it needs to be.

options.text: Resolve the most urgent request in this reply and ask the customer to open separate tickets for the other two
options.why: Splitting the conversation meets the time target by dropping work rather than restructuring it. The customer has to repeat themselves twice, and total time to resolve all three requests goes up.

explain: Binding constraint: confirmations depend on the email change, while the billing check, order trace and email change are independent of each other. Decompose by dependency: run every independent step as a parallel section and gate only the dependent step, sending notices, behind the one it needs.

signals: attributable to the engineer who ran them
stem: Dunmore Freight's platform team wants every engineer who clones the routing-service repository to get the same GitHub MCP server in Claude Code without anyone hand-configuring the server. The server runs locally over stdio and authenticates only with a GitHub personal access token read from its environment. Security policy says no credential may be committed to version control, and actions taken through the server must be attributable to the engineer who ran them. New hires join every month, so the team wants onboarding to stay light.
ask: Which configuration BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Have each engineer add the server to their own `~/.claude.json` with a personal token pasted into the entry
options.why: User-scope config never propagates, so every engineer repeats the setup by hand and configurations drift over time. It keeps the token out of Git but fails the requirement that nobody hand-configures the server.

options.text: Commit `.mcp.json` with one shared team service-account token inside it, so onboarding needs no steps
options.why: It commits a credential, breaking policy outright, and one shared identity makes every action look like the service account. Attribution is lost, and the token likely carries broader permissions than any single engineer needs.

options.text: Ship a setup script that writes the server into each engineer's user config the first time they clone
options.why: A script still writes to user scope, so it is a manual step every hire must remember, and later changes to the server never reach existing machines. Committed project config removes both problems.

options.text: Commit `.mcp.json` using `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` expansion and have each engineer export a personal token
options.why: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` travels with the repository, and `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` expansion in the server's `env` block keeps the secret out of Git. Each engineer's own token means the server acts with that person's GitHub permissions, so actions stay attributable.

explain: Binding constraints: no committed credentials and per-engineer attribution. Commit the shared stdio server in project-scoped .mcp.json with ${GITHUB_TOKEN} expansion in its env block, so each engineer supplies a personal token, which keeps secrets out of Git and has the server act with that engineer's own permissions.

stem: Norrvik Automation's platform lead kept the team's Claude Code conventions in her own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`: test commands, naming rules and a line telling Claude never to read `.env` files. New hires who clone the repository report that Claude ignores the conventions, and one session opened a `.env` file while debugging. The security lead says the `.env` ban must hold on every run for everyone working in this repository. The conventions need to reach every clone and change through pull-request review. Everyone starts Claude Code from the repository root, and nothing is required for other repositories.
ask: Which change BEST meets both requirements?

options.text: Add an `@~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` import line to a committed project CLAUDE.md so that each clone pulls in her file
options.why: Imports exist and load at launch, but `~` resolves to each reader's own home directory, so teammates import their own file or nothing. Even where it resolves, the imported `.env` line is still advisory context that cannot stop a read.

options.text: Commit the conventions as project CLAUDE.md and put a `Read(**/.env)` deny rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`
options.why: The conventions half is right, but local settings are personal: `.claude/settings.local.json` applies to one person in one project and Claude Code keeps it out of git. The deny rule never reaches a clone or passes through review, so teammates can still open `.env`.

options.text: Move the conventions and the `.env` rule into a committed project CLAUDE.md that loads for every clone
options.why: This fixes reach for the conventions, which is correct, but CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement. A rule that must hold on every run needs a permission rule or hook that blocks the read whatever Claude decides.

options.text: Commit the conventions as project CLAUDE.md and put a `Read(**/.env)` deny rule in `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: Project CLAUDE.md is version-controlled, loads for every clone and changes through review, which suits conventions. A `Read(**/.env)` deny rule in the shared, committed `.claude/settings.json` blocks any `.env` under the repository for Claude's file tools and commands such as `cat`, whatever Claude decides, and enabling the sandbox extends the block to every sandboxed shell process.

explain: Binding constraints: the conventions must reach every clone and the `.env` ban must hold on every run. Both belong in committed project files, CLAUDE.md for conventions and `.claude/settings.json` for the deny rule, because user and local scope never propagate; a must-hold rule needs a permission rule or hook because CLAUDE.md is advisory. Managed settings would be needed only if the ban had to be non-overridable on every machine.

signals: Two rewrites of the prose instruction changed nothing
stem: Aldermoor Air, a regional airline, runs a production prompt that reads customer rebooking emails and fills a `travel_date` field in `YYYY-MM-DD` for its reservation system. Emails say things like 'next Friday', 'the 3rd' or '03/04', from both UK and US customers, and the prompt passes in each email's sent date and the sender's country. Output is inconsistent: some dates are ISO, some are `MM/DD/YYYY`, and a few return 'next Friday' unchanged. The team ruled out a regex or date library because the meaning depends on context. Two rewrites of the prose instruction changed nothing.
ask: Which change is MOST likely to make the output consistent?

options.text: Move the prompt to the largest model tier so its stronger reasoning follows the date instruction more reliably
options.why: Nothing shows a capability gap: the model reads the emails and fails on an underspecified target. A bigger tier costs more per email and still has to guess how '03/04' from a UK sender should be written.

options.text: Add three to five varied email-to-date examples, with relative and locale-ambiguous phrases and ISO output
options.why: Examples show the exact target where prose leaves room to guess: 'next Friday' resolved from the sent date, '03/04' read day-first for a UK sender. Three to five diverse examples is the usual range for fixing format and structure.

options.text: Restate the ISO rule in capitals at both the start and the end of the prompt, marked clearly as mandatory
options.why: Emphasis tells the model the rule matters, which it already knows. It does not show how to resolve a relative phrase or a locale-ambiguous date, so the same inconsistent guesses continue.

options.text: Paste the ISO 8601 standard and reference tables of national date orders and relative-date terms into the prompt
options.why: More reference text adds tokens without demonstrating the transformation. The model already knows ISO 8601, what 'next Friday' means and that UK senders write the day first; what it lacks is a worked picture of how this team maps each kind of phrase to the field.

explain: Binding constraint: the input is context-dependent free text, so a deterministic parser is out and the defect is an underspecified output. Few-shot examples fix format and structure where prose has failed; a schema could force the YYYY-MM-DD shape, but only examples show how to resolve 'next Friday' or '03/04' for this sender. Capitals, repetition, reference dumps and bigger tiers do not resolve the ambiguity.

stem: Veltmoor Health's CI pipeline runs a Claude security review prompt on every pull request. It flags 60% of PRs for 'potential vulnerabilities', and nearly all flags land on input-validation patterns the security team has approved as acceptable. Developers now skip the reports. Adding 'only report high-confidence findings' to the prompt had no measurable effect. While the team decides what to do, the security category has already been switched to non-blocking, and a set of 200 PRs labelled by the security team is available.
ask: What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Spell out reportable versus approved patterns with code examples of each, then re-measure on the labelled PRs
options.why: 'High confidence' names no boundary. Explicit criteria with contrasting examples tell the model what counts as a positive, and the 200 labelled PRs show whether the false-positive rate really fell before blocking is restored.

options.text: Have Claude score its confidence in each finding and pick the cutoff that best matches the 200 labelled PRs
options.why: Tuning the cutoff on labelled data still thresholds the model's own scores, and it is confident about the approved patterns because nobody has told it they are approved, as the failed 'high-confidence' line showed. A cutoff low enough to drop them also drops real findings.

options.text: Move the security review to a larger model tier whose stronger judgement should separate real flaws from approved code
options.why: The model is not short of reasoning; it has never been told which patterns the team approves. A larger tier costs more per PR and still has no definition of acceptable to work from.

options.text: Delete the security category from the review prompt so developers see only the style and logic findings they trust
options.why: Cutting the category ends the noise and also ends the security review the pipeline exists to provide. The failure is imprecise criteria, which can be fixed without removing required coverage.

explain: Binding constraint: precision on a check developers must trust, with labelled data available to prove it. A system prompt steers only as well as it defines its target, so replace vague qualifiers with explicit reportable-versus-acceptable criteria and examples, then measure against the labelled set before restoring blocking.

signals: already lists the four required fields in detail
stem: Quillstack, a SaaS vendor, runs Claude Code in CI to post review comments on pull requests. The system prompt already lists the four required fields in detail (file path, line number, issue, suggested fix), yet formatting still varies: some comments are bullet lists with every field, others are prose paragraphs, and some give a vague summary with no line number. The content is usually accurate. Developers want every comment in one scannable layout so they can act on it quickly.
ask: Which change is MOST likely to produce the consistent layout?

options.text: Restate the four-field list in capitals at the end of the prompt and label it as the mandatory format
options.why: The field list is already in the prompt, so repeating it louder adds emphasis but no information. The model still has to guess what a finished comment looks like, and the variation continues.

options.text: Add `--output-format json` to the CI command so each review comment comes back in the same field structure
options.why: That flag wraps the run's final result and metadata in a JSON envelope; the comment text inside is still whatever prose the model wrote. Only the separate `--json-schema` flag constrains structure, and this option does not use it.

options.text: Add three to five complete example comments in the target layout, each covering a different kind of issue
options.why: Worked examples show the exact layout, field order and level of detail across issue types, which a field list alone has not conveyed. Format drift with correct content is the classic case for few-shot examples, and three to five varied examples is the usual range.

options.text: Ask Claude to re-read each comment against the field list and rewrite any that miss a field before it is posted
options.why: The checker works from the same field list that has not produced consistency, so it inherits the same unclear picture of the target, and it adds a second pass per comment. Examples fix the cause at generation.

explain: Binding constraint: the audience needs one actionable layout, and a detailed field list has already failed to deliver it. When content is right but format drifts, few-shot examples are the technique that fixes format and structure; louder instructions, output envelopes and self-checks do not show the target.

stem: Kessendale Legal uses Claude to classify contract clauses into a fixed taxonomy for a due-diligence tool. An eval on 400 labelled clauses shows 97% accuracy on clauses that fit one category but about 60% on clauses that could fit two, such as a termination clause that also contains force majeure language. The category definitions in the prompt are accurate, and the current few-shot examples are all clean single-category clauses. Associates reviewing the misclassified clauses agree on the right category and can explain why. New contracts keep producing category pairings that no fixed example set will cover.
ask: Which change BEST targets the failing slice?

options.text: Add more clean single-category examples so the model sees each category's core pattern more sharply
options.why: More of what already works reinforces the 97% slice. Clean examples never show a clause straddling two categories, so the model still has no pattern for the cases that are failing.

options.text: Add clauses that span two categories as new examples, each one labelled with its correct category only
options.why: Boundary examples are the right slice, but this assumes a bare label conveys the deciding factor. The model sees which category a straddling clause went to, not why, so the new pairings the stem expects are still guessed.

options.text: Add a confidence field and route clauses the model rates as unsure to associates, leaving the prompt unchanged
options.why: Human review is a sound safeguard, but a self-rated field is uncalibrated and the prompt never improves. The associates' explanations, the signal that would teach the model, go unused.

options.text: Add worked examples of clauses that span two categories, each showing the reasoning for the one chosen
options.why: The failing slice is boundary cases, so the examples must be boundary cases. Showing the associates' reasoning teaches the feature that decides the category, which carries over to pairings the examples do not cover, and the 400-clause eval, kept separate from the examples, can confirm the slice improves.

explain: Binding constraint: the accuracy gap sits in one slice, clauses that fit two categories, and new pairings keep appearing. Examples should cover the cases that fail, with the reasoning that resolves them; clean examples, bare labels or self-rated routing leave the model's judgement on unseen boundary clauses unchanged.

stem: Orlenvik Home, an online furniture retailer, extracts product attributes from supplier spec sheets. The prompt asks Claude to return JSON inside a code block, and about 3% of responses break the downstream parser with missing commas or unescaped quotes. Each failure needs manual reprocessing. Responses end well under the max_tokens limit, so nothing is being cut off. The catalogue team needs every response to parse, because the loader rejects a whole batch when one record is malformed.
ask: What is the MOST reliable way to stop the parse failures?

options.text: Validate each response with a JSON parser and re-run the prompt up to three times whenever parsing fails
options.why: Retries catch failures after they happen, adding latency and cost, and a record can still fail every attempt. They lower the rate without removing the cause, which is unconstrained generation of free-text JSON.

options.text: Use structured outputs: a JSON schema in `output_config.format`, or `strict: true` on the extraction tool
options.why: With a JSON schema in `output_config.format` or `strict: true` on the tool, constrained decoding keeps responses schema-valid, so parsing stops being probabilistic. Refusals and max_tokens stops remain separate `stop_reason` checks.

options.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt that the response must be valid JSON and to check its syntax before replying
options.why: An instruction raises the odds of valid output but cannot make it hold every time, and the stem needs every record to parse. Self-checking is still the same unconstrained generation the errors came from.

options.text: Run a regex repair step that fixes missing commas and unescaped quotes before the output reaches the parser
options.why: This assumes the malformations follow a few repeatable patterns. Real JSON breakage is open-ended, a regex can corrupt valid strings, and each new error shape needs another rule.

explain: Binding constraint: every response must parse, so validity has to be enforced by the decoder, not requested of the model. Structured outputs (a JSON-schema output format or strict tool use) constrain generation to the schema; prompt instructions, retries and regex repair only lower the failure rate.

signals: no invoice that fails it may post
stem: Marrowby County's accounts payable pipeline extracts invoices with strict tool use, and extractions that pass validation post to the payment system automatically. About 8% fail a business-rule check: the line items do not sum to `total_amount`. Spot checks confirm the source totals are correct; the errors come from misread line items, and the documents are complete and legible. The controller wants the check to stay a real control: no invoice that fails it may post, and staff time should go only where automation cannot fix the record.
ask: Which retry design BEST fits these requirements?

options.text: Retry each failing invoice up to three times with the same prompt and keep the first result that reconciles
options.why: This assumes the misread is random, but the same document and prompt tend to reproduce the same misread, so blind retries rarely converge. Nothing tells the model what failed, and each attempt spends calls without adding information.

options.text: Send every invoice that fails the check straight to accounts payable staff for manual keying, with no retry
options.why: Human review belongs in the design, as the fallback once feedback retries fail. Sending the whole 8% straight to staff spends their time on records the model could correct from a specific error message.

options.text: Re-extract given the failed result and exact mismatch, re-run the check, and route to staff after two misses
options.why: The data is present, so naming the discrepancy ('line items sum to X, total is Y') sends the model back to the document to find the misread line. Each retry must pass the same check before it posts, and the bounded retry hands persistent failures to people.

options.text: Overwrite `total_amount` with the sum of the extracted line items and let the invoice post with no flag raised
options.why: The source totals are the correct values and the line items are the misread part, so this replaces a right number with a wrong one. The check can then never fail, which turns the control into a paper gate.

explain: Binding constraint: no invoice that fails the check may post, so the check must refuse the record until it is fixed. Retry by re-extracting with the specific error as feedback while the invoice stays blocked, re-run the same check on each attempt, and fail closed to human review after a bounded number of tries; never coerce values so that the check passes.

signals: an engineer reviewing the modules afterwards
stem: Quenby Stream's code-generation pipeline asks Claude to write a service module from a spec and then, in the same conversation, to review that module for bugs before a human approves the merge. The reviews usually return 'no significant issues' with a few style notes. Over the last month QA has traced six production defects to logic errors in these modules, and an engineer reviewing the modules afterwards found most of them within minutes. Modules average about 300 lines.
ask: What is the MOST likely cause, and which change addresses it?

options.text: The context is overloaded; generate modules in smaller chunks so the review step has less code to hold at once
options.why: A 300-line module is small for current context windows, and nothing in the stem points to length. The engineer caught the errors without the generation context, which implicates shared reasoning, not volume.

options.text: The reviewer shares the generator's reasoning; give the code and spec to a separate instance with no history
options.why: A reviewer that carries the generation context tends to confirm its own choices. A fresh instance that sees only the code and spec reads it the way the engineer did, which is why it catches what self-review misses.

options.text: Reviews lack specialist depth; add security, style and logic reviewer agents, one per owning team, in the same thread
options.why: Splitting by team adds agents without adding independence. Every reviewer still sits in the conversation that wrote the code, so each inherits the assumptions that let the logic errors through.

options.text: The review model is too weak; keep the review in the same conversation but run it on a larger model tier
options.why: Nothing shows a capability gap: an engineer found the errors within minutes. A larger model reviewing inside the same conversation still carries the reasoning that produced the bugs, so it tends to confirm them.

explain: Binding constraint: the review must be independent of the reasoning that produced the code. Self-review in the generating context tends to confirm its own decisions, so a second instance given only the code and spec is a justified split, whereas per-team agents or a bigger tier in the same context are not.

signals: the prompt and model have not changed
stem: Tallisford Lending extracts fields from loan summaries into its underwriting system. In this month's batch, the `guarantor_address` field comes back null on every record. Each summary has already been retried three times with the original document and the validation error in the prompt, and the value is still null. Other fields in the same summaries extract correctly, and the prompt and model have not changed since last month's batch, which extracted guarantor addresses without trouble.
ask: What should the team investigate FIRST, before scheduling further retries?

options.text: Whether the validation error message sent with each retry names the `guarantor_address` field correctly
options.why: This assumes the retry feedback is the fault, but the first pass returned null before any error was sent, and a correctly worded error cannot produce a value that is not in the document. It examines the retry, not why the field is empty.

options.text: Whether a larger model tier has the reasoning capacity to locate the field that the current tier keeps missing
options.why: The same model extracted this field last month and still extracts every other field in these summaries. The model layer did not change, so it is the least likely place for the fault.

options.text: Whether making `guarantor_address` optional in the schema would let these summaries pass validation downstream
options.why: A nullable field may well be part of the eventual fix, but doing it first skips the question of where the address actually is, and underwriting would silently receive incomplete records.

options.text: Whether this batch's summaries actually contain a guarantor address, or whether their layout has changed
options.why: Retries help only when the answer is in the input. If the new summaries now point to a separate exhibit, the fix is to retrieve that exhibit and allow a documented null; if the layout moved the address, the prompt needs to show where it now sits.

explain: Binding constraint: diagnose what changed before trying more. With the prompt and model unchanged and other fields fine, the likeliest fault is that this batch's documents lack the value, so confirm presence first; if it lives in an exhibit, retrieve the exhibit and make the field nullable rather than retrying.

signals: folded into a running summary that is rewritten
stem: Veyrand Mobile's support agent handles billing disputes that often run past 20 turns. To control cost, turns older than 10 are folded into a running summary that is rewritten as the chat grows. Early in one chat, a customer said they were charged $847.50 on 3 March for a plan they cancelled on 28 February. By turn 16 the agent refers only to 'the overcharge from last month', quotes no amount, and the customer disputes its account of the case. The budget for each conversation is fixed.
ask: Which change BEST prevents this without dropping the cost control?

options.text: Keep amounts, dates and account IDs in a structured case-facts block re-sent each turn, outside the summary
options.why: Transactional facts extracted once and carried verbatim on each turn cannot be paraphrased away by the running summary. The block is small, so the cost control on older turns stays in place.

options.text: Instruct the summariser to copy every amount, date and account ID verbatim into its running summary
options.why: Each rewrite re-summarises the summary, so the instruction raises the odds of keeping '$847.50 on 3 March' but cannot guarantee it, and nothing gives those values a fixed slot. A facts block extracted once and re-sent unchanged cannot drift.

options.text: Move the agent to a larger tier with a bigger context window and stop summarising the conversation history
options.why: The window did not lose the figure; the summary did. Dropping summarisation would keep it, but at exactly the cost the team set out to control, and a larger tier also raises the price per token.

options.text: Instruct the agent to re-read the whole conversation carefully before it replies to each new customer message
options.why: This assumes the early turns are still in context. They have been folded into the summary, so there is nothing verbatim to re-read, and the instruction cannot recover the amount.

explain: Binding constraint: the cost control stays, so older turns will keep being summarised. Precise transactional facts belong in a structured block re-sent every turn, because summaries paraphrase numbers and dates; a verbatim instruction to the summariser, a bigger window or a re-read instruction does not protect them.

signals: Transfer me to a human agent now
should not have had to ask twice
stem: Harlow Broadband's support agent can resolve routine billing adjustments end to end with its own tools. A customer's first message reads: "Transfer me to a human agent now. I have been fighting this billing error for three weeks." The agent classifies the case as a two-step adjustment, replies that it can fix this right away, and starts pulling the account. The customer repeats the transfer request, then leaves a one-star survey saying they should not have had to ask twice. The support lead is now rewriting the rule that decides when the agent hands a chat to a person.
ask: Which handoff rule BEST fixes this failure?

options.text: Let the agent judge from the customer's tone each turn whether a person is really needed
options.why: Judging tone is the model deciding when a human is needed, a signal that is never validated. Here the customer has already stated the need outright, so nothing needs inferring, and a misread tone would override a clear request.

options.text: Hand off on any explicit request for a person, before investigating or offering a fix
options.why: A stated request for a person is an explicit, policy-defined trigger that needs no interpretation. Honouring it on first ask, with the case context passed to the human, is predictable and auditable, and it respects the customer's choice even when the agent could have solved the issue.

options.text: Offer the fix once, then hand off right away if the customer repeats the request
options.why: Offering once suits a frustrated customer who has not asked for anyone. This customer's first message asked for a person outright, so even one fix attempt overrides the request and makes them ask twice, the exact complaint behind the one-star survey.

options.text: Keep automated handling for any case within the agent's tested capability, with an apology
options.why: Capability decides what the agent may do, not whether the customer must accept it. Choosing automation on the customer's behalf after an explicit request takes the decision away from its owner, and an apology does not change that.

explain: Binding constraint: an explicit request for a person must trigger a handoff the first time it is made. Escalation triggers should be explicit, policy-defined signals such as a stated request, a policy rule or a failed check, never sentiment scores or the model's own confidence. Offering a fix first, then escalating on repetition, is for frustrated customers who have not asked for a person.

signals: returned status "success" with an empty results list
no sign that anything had failed
stem: Harrowgate Bank's strategy team uses a coordinator agent that hands research subtopics to worker subagents and passes their results to a synthesis step. During a competitor analysis, the web search subagent hit a timeout. Its handler caught the error and returned status "success" with an empty results list. The final report went out with no competitor section and no sign that anything had failed. The team lead wants the coordinator to be able to react when a worker fails.
ask: Which change BEST lets the coordinator recover from failures like this?

options.text: Have the synthesis agent spot missing sections and call the search subagent again directly
options.why: This detects the gap downstream instead of stopping the misreport at its source. The synthesis agent lacks the coordinator's plan and budget, and a direct call bypasses the orchestrator that owns retries, so failures stay hidden from the component meant to handle them.

options.text: Raise the search timeout so that the subagent rarely fails before real results arrive
options.why: A longer timeout makes this particular failure rarer but leaves the contract unchanged. The next timeout, rate limit or outage would again arrive as an empty success, so a report could still ship silently incomplete.

options.text: Make the coordinator treat every empty result as a failure and rerun that worker automatically
options.why: This assumes an empty list always means failure. A legitimate search can find nothing, so reruns would waste cost and can loop, and the coordinator still could not tell a timeout from a genuine absence of results or explain the gap.

options.text: Return a typed error with the failure type, a retryable flag and any partial results gathered
options.why: A structured error, giving the failure type, whether a retry is safe and what was gathered, lets the coordinator retry, route to another source, or proceed and annotate the coverage gap. Failure stays visible instead of passing as finished work.

explain: Binding constraint: the coordinator can only recover from failures it can see. A subagent's return contract must separate failure from an empty result, carrying the error type, retryability and partial results, so the coordinator can retry, reroute or annotate the coverage gap instead of passing incomplete work as complete. Transient faults can be retried inside the subagent first; only unresolved failures need to reach the coordinator.

signals: will depend on the same findings
stem: Orrin Health's security team runs a multi-phase audit of its patient portal code with an Agent SDK agent. In phase one, over about 45 minutes, the agent read files, traced call chains and noted that the login service signs tokens with a custom routine rather than a standard JWT library. Early in phase two, a vulnerability review of the authentication module, the agent describes that module as "using standard JWT patterns." Phase three, a remediation plan, will depend on the same findings.
ask: Which technique BEST keeps key findings intact across the phase boundaries?

options.text: Have the agent record its findings in a notes file each phase and load it when the next one starts
options.why: Structured note-taking keeps findings outside the context window, so they survive compaction or a new session exactly as written. The custom signing detail is recorded once and reloaded at each phase start, which costs little context.

options.text: Start each phase in a fresh session and rely on the agent to re-derive the earlier findings
options.why: A clean context avoids the drift, but this depends on the agent rediscovering every finding unaided. That repeats 45 minutes of exploration per phase, and nothing guarantees it notices the custom signing routine a second time.

options.text: Raise the output token limit so that more of the session history can stay in context without compression
options.why: The output token limit caps the length of each response, not the size of the context window, so this changes nothing about what the agent remembers. Even a larger window would leave the finding buried mid-history, where recall is weakest.

options.text: Run a default compaction before each phase and let the agent re-read files whenever it needs detail
options.why: Compaction is a valid long-session technique, but a default summary does not know which detail matters and can flatten the custom routine into a generic label. Re-reading files then spends tokens recovering what a note would have kept.

explain: Binding constraint: specific findings must survive intact across several phases.
