Anthropic names three long-horizon context techniques, compaction, structured note-taking and sub-agent architectures; note-taking wins here because findings persist verbatim outside the window, while compaction without explicit keep instructions is lossy and a higher output token limit does not enlarge the context.

signals: having the model score each extraction
stem: Pellham Assurance extracts fields from claim documents with Claude and wants high-confidence extractions to post automatically while the rest go to adjusters. Average field accuracy on last month's sample was high. A developer proposes adding a confidence field to the output schema, having the model score each extraction from 0 to 1, and auto-posting anything above 0.9. Two of the fields, payout amount and policy number, feed straight into payments.
ask: Which response to the developer's proposal is BEST?

options.text: Raise the cut-off to 0.95 so that only the most certain self-scored extractions post automatically
options.why: A higher number feels safer, but nobody has checked what any self-score means against real outcomes. Without labelled data, 0.95 is as arbitrary as 0.9, and payment fields could still post wrongly behind a high self-score.

options.text: Have the model re-check every field it scored below 0.9 before any of them reach an adjuster
options.why: The same model re-grading its own work shares its blind spots, so confident errors stay confident and are never re-checked. The gate still rests on the model's self-assessment rather than on any validated signal.

options.text: Gate on per-field signals checked against labelled outcomes, and send payment fields to review
options.why: A model's stated confidence is not evidence until it is calibrated per field against labelled outcomes. Route on signals checked that way, such as validation failures or a calibrated score. Payment fields go to review whatever the score until their calibrated error rate is shown to be acceptable, since an error there moves money.

options.text: Move extraction to a larger model whose stated confidence tracks its real accuracy more closely
options.why: A bigger tier may extract more accurately, but its self-reported confidence is still unvalidated. The defect is the routing signal, not the model size, and payment fields would still auto-post on the model's word.

explain: Binding constraint: an auto-post gate needs evidence that its signal predicts correctness. An uncalibrated self-score provides no such evidence; a per-field score becomes usable only once its thresholds are calibrated against labelled outcomes. High-impact fields such as payout amount go to review on the cost of error, whatever any score says, so payments do not auto-post yet.

signals: traceable to its original source before release
stem: Linfield Policy Office runs five research subagents over different source sets, and a synthesis agent merges their summaries into briefings for ministers. A published briefing stated that "telehealth use in rural clinics reached 38% in 2024" with no citation. A reviewer could not trace the figure because the subagents' outputs were discarded after synthesis. The office now requires every figure in a briefing to be traceable to its original source before release.
ask: Which pipeline change BEST meets the new requirement?

options.text: Add a Sources consulted section listing every document the subagents accessed during research
options.why: A bibliography shows what was read, not which source backs which figure. A reviewer checking the 38% claim would still have to hunt through every listed document, so the briefing is no more traceable claim by claim.

options.text: Have subagents return claim-to-source mappings and make synthesis carry each into the report
options.why: Provenance is lost where summaries compress findings. Having each subagent return claim, source and excerpt together, and requiring synthesis to keep that mapping, prevents the loss at its source so every figure arrives traceable. Citations make claims checkable, not automatically correct.

options.text: Before release, have the synthesis agent search the web for a source that supports each claim
options.why: Finding support after the fact is detection, not prevention, and it can attach a source that agrees with the figure but is not where it came from. A mismatched citation looks traceable while hiding the real origin.

options.text: Store all raw subagent outputs in a log so that reviewers can search them when a claim is queried
options.why: Keeping raw outputs helps an investigation, but it assumes a reviewer can match each figure to the right output by searching. The briefing itself still carries no provenance, and every query becomes manual archaeology.

explain: Binding constraint: each figure must be traceable to its origin before release. Prevention beats detection: provenance belongs in the inter-agent data contract, carried from subagent to report, because sources attached after synthesis can mismatch the real origin and a raw-output archive leaves the briefing itself untraced.

stem: Corliss & Vane, a litigation firm, runs a research coordinator that spawns subagents for case-law subtopics. To give them "full context," the coordinator passes its entire conversation history, including every earlier subagent report, into each new subagent. On long matters, subagents now run slower, cost more per call, and drift into subtopics that other subagents already covered. The practice manager wants a fix before the system is rolled out to more matters.
ask: Which change BEST addresses the slowdown, cost and drift together?

options.text: Move the subagents to a 1M-token context model so the full history fits without truncation
options.why: A larger window removes truncation but not the waste. Every subagent still processes and is billed for the repeated history, at cache rates at best, longer inputs add latency, and a longer mix of irrelevant reports dilutes focus further rather than restoring it.

options.text: Keep sending the full history, and tell each subagent to ignore sections outside its subtopic
options.why: An instruction to ignore text does not remove it. The tokens are still processed and billed on every call, at cache rates at best, and the model can still be pulled toward other subtopics, so cost, latency and drift all persist.

options.text: Use fewer subagents per matter so that the shared history is passed along fewer times
options.why: Fewer subagents cuts the repetition count but leaves each one with the same bloated input, and it gives up the parallel coverage that justified subagents. It trades breadth for a partial cost win without fixing focus.

options.text: Give each subagent a brief with the goal, facts, constraints and boundaries of its subtopic
options.why: A fresh subagent sees only what the coordinator puts in its prompt. A scoped brief spends each subagent's context on its own task, which cuts input tokens, latency and cost per call, and stating the subtopic's boundaries keeps it off ground other subagents already cover.

explain: Binding constraint: cost and latency scale with what every subagent is sent. The coordinator should pass each subagent only the goal, constraints, facts, scope boundaries and return format its subtask needs, because repeated history is processed and billed on every call, even at cache rates, slows each run, and dilutes focus whatever the window size.

stem: Talbrook Energy handles billing disputes with two agents. The investigation agent reads account history and holds no payment tools; for least-privilege reasons, only the resolution agent can issue refunds. Today the handoff is a single prose message such as "Customer verified, charge looks wrong, please refund." On accounts with several recent charges, the resolution agent sometimes refunds the wrong one, and on others it repeats the whole identity check from scratch.
ask: Which change BEST makes this handoff reliable?

options.text: Send a structured payload with customer ID, order ID, completed steps and the requested action
options.why: Explicit identifiers remove the guesswork that picks the wrong charge, and the completed-steps field stops needless re-verification. The refund tool should still confirm in code, against the system-of-record verification record the payload references, that the order belongs to that customer before any money moves.

options.text: Ask the investigation agent to write fuller handoff messages that restate each finding in detail
options.why: More prose adds words without adding structure. The order ID can still be missing or ambiguous among several charges, and the resolution agent still has to infer which verification steps were completed.

options.text: Merge the two agents into one so that no handoff is needed anywhere in the dispute workflow
options.why: Merging removes the handoff but also the least-privilege split that justifies two agents. The component reading account history would then hold refund power, one over-privileged identity that widens the blast radius of any mistake.

options.text: Have the resolution agent re-verify the customer and re-derive the disputed order on every case
options.why: This assumes the resolution agent can reliably work out which charge is disputed from account data alone, which is exactly what fails on multi-charge accounts. It also discards completed work. An in-code ownership check inside the refund tool is different and worth keeping.

explain: Binding constraint: refunds move money and are hard to reverse, so the receiving agent must not guess. A handoff between agents should carry explicit identifiers and completed-step state in a structured payload, and whatever the payload says, the refund tool should confirm in code, against the system-of-record verification record, that the order belongs to that customer before it acts.

signals: Both call the same orders API
stem: Fenwick Outfitters' support agent has grown to 38 tools as teams added features over the past year, and wrong-tool calls are rising. The worst pair is `find_order`, described as "look up an order," and `search_orders`, described as "search for orders." Both call the same orders API. The agent uses them interchangeably, often calling `search_orders` with a known order ID and then mishandling the list that comes back.
ask: Which change BEST fixes the selection errors for this pair?

options.text: Add a routing paragraph to the system prompt telling the agent which of the two tools to use and when
options.why: Routing prose patches the ambiguity from outside the tools and grows with every new overlap. The two near-identical tools stay in a 38-tool catalogue, so selection remains fragile and the prompt gets longer each time.

options.text: Shorten both tool descriptions so that the large catalogue uses fewer tokens on every request
options.why: Token cost is not the defect here. The descriptions are already too vague to choose between, so cutting them further removes the little selection information they carry and makes wrong picks more likely.

options.text: Replace both with one `get_orders` tool that always returns a list and documents its ID and filter inputs
options.why: Both tools hit the same API, so one is a duplicate that adds choice without adding capability. One tool with documented ID and filter inputs removes the ambiguous choice, and one list shape, holding one order or many, removes the mishandled return. It does one job, so it is not a mode-switch mega-tool.

options.text: Make `search_orders` return only its first match so that both tools give back the same shape
options.why: Matching the return shapes hides the symptom by throwing away real results. Filtered searches that legitimately match several orders would silently lose data, and the agent still has two indistinguishable tools to choose between.

explain: Binding constraint: selection gets harder with every overlapping tool in a growing catalogue. Capability bloat is fixed by reducing and separating what the agent sees: delete duplicate tools, give the survivor one consistent return shape, and sharpen real boundaries, rather than adding routing prose, trimming descriptions or truncating results.

stem: Kestrel Learning's platform team wants every engineer who clones the course-platform repository to get the same MCP server for the internal issue tracker, without configuring it by hand. The server needs an API token, which must not be committed to the repository. The secrets manager already sets the token as an environment variable on each engineer's machine, and the team reviews all shared tooling changes through pull requests.
ask: Which way of distributing the server configuration is BEST?

options.text: Have each engineer add the server to their user-level config by following steps in the README
options.why: User-level config lives on one machine and never reaches teammates, so every new hire repeats the setup and versions drift. It also skips the pull-request review the team uses for shared tooling.

options.text: Commit a project `.mcp.json` that pulls the token in through `${TRACKER_TOKEN}` expansion
options.why: A committed project .mcp.json travels with every clone and changes through review, while ${VAR} expansion keeps the secret in each machine's environment. Interactive sessions ask each engineer to approve the project server on first use; -p runs, and SDK runs that load project settings, connect it without asking.

options.text: Commit the project config with the token written inline, since the repository itself is private
options.why: Private is not secret: the token lands in git history, every clone and fork, and any log that prints config. Rotating it means rewriting history, and the stem rules out committing it at all.

options.text: Describe the server and its launch command in `CLAUDE.md` so Claude registers it in every session
options.why: CLAUDE.md is instruction context, not configuration. It registers nothing by itself; at best it asks Claude to run a setup command each session, which is unreviewed, needs permission and may not happen, so the tracker tools are not reliably available.

explain: Binding constraint: one configuration must reach every clone without exposing the token. Team-wide behaviour belongs in version-controlled project config, with secrets pulled from each machine's environment through ${VAR} expansion; user-level config never propagates, CLAUDE.md registers nothing by itself, and a private repository is not a secret store.

stem: Dunmore Rail Freight is adding a Claude Code review step to the CI pipeline for pull requests, including those from outside contributors. The job must run unattended, never stop for a confirmation prompt, and never push commits or edit files under .github/workflows. It only needs to read the diff, run the linter and post review comments. A pull request can change any file in the repository, including .mcp.json and the .claude directory.
ask: Which configuration BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Run headless with --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit" so that no permission prompt can ever stall the job
options.why: This meets the no-prompt requirement by pre-approving every shell command and edit, which leaves only the model's judgment between a hostile diff and a git push or workflow edit. Without bare mode, the checkout's hooks and .mcp.json servers also run.

options.text: Bypass all permission checks, since the runner is a throwaway container rebuilt from scratch for each job
options.why: This assumes the only possible damage is inside the container. The job holds repository credentials, so an unchecked run, perhaps steered by a malicious diff, can push commits or change workflows on shared systems that outlive the container.

options.text: Rely on the deny rules for git push and workflow edits in the repository's committed .claude settings
options.why: Committed project settings are part of the pull request under review, so an outside contributor can weaken them. Without bare mode, a -p run also executes project hooks and .mcp.json servers from the checkout with no trust dialog.

options.text: Run in bare -p mode with passed-in rules allowing only read, lint and comment, on a token that cannot push
options.why: Bare mode skips the checkout's hooks, skills, plugins, .mcp.json servers and CLAUDE.md, and dontAsk denies, without prompting, any call that needs approval and is not on the passed-in allowlist. Deny rules govern only Claude's own calls, and the linter runs PR-controlled config, so the token is what makes a push impossible. Excluding project setting sources also blocks their env block.

explain: Binding constraint: the job processes untrusted pull-request content with credentials that could push. Load only config the job passes in (bare mode, with project setting sources excluded because their env block still applies), use dontAsk with an allowlist of the review's tools, and give the job a token that cannot push, since the linter runs PR-controlled code that permission rules do not govern.
